items.title: Operators of death: checked arithmetic in Rust
items.author: John Arundel
items.content:
Everything has its limits, even Rust, and this applies to numeric types too. They always have a fixed —a fixed number of bits—and that means there’s a limit to how large a number they can represent. When the result of a sum is bigger than that maximum value for the type, we can no longer represent it correctly: a problem called .

Spells of protection from arithmetic overflow

You probably know that numbers (and everything else) are represented internally in the computer using binary . Rust’s various numeric data types each have a fixed number of bits with which to represent a number: for example, the type represents a number using 8 bits. That’s because the compiler needs to know how much memory space to reserve for each of the data values in your program.

But just as there’s only so large a number you can write down in decimal on a fixed-width piece of paper, there’s only so large a number you can store as a Rust value using a fixed number of bits. Let’s see if we can figure out what that number is.

The relationship between the of a data type—the number of bits it uses to store a value—and the range of values it can represent is straightforward, but let’s think our way into it a little.

Suppose we had only one bit available to represent numbers. That would be tough, but we could still do something, and it’s the easiest case to start with.

A single binary bit can take one of two possible values (hence “binary”). It’s up to us what we use for these values: “true or false”, “on or off”, “set or clear”, “high or low” are all used in various contexts. But for this discussion let’s call them 0 or 1.

How many different number values can we represent with a 1-bit type? The answer is two. Easy, right? The choice of which numbers these two values represent is purely arbitrary. It doesn’t have to be 0 and 1, but let’s go with that for simplicity.

Now suppose we widen our type a little, to two bits. How many possible values can we represent now? Maybe you see the answer right away, but let’s write out all the possibilities to be clear:

Again, the precise decimal numbers that we assign to each permutation of the bits are an arbitrary choice, and we might choose differently depending on the situation.

With the scheme we’ve outlined so far, we can only represent zero or positive numbers (called representation), but that’s okay; there are other schemes. Let’s see how this one changes as we add more bits to the representation.

How about a three-bit type? Can you say what the —the number of possible values—is now? If you guessed “six”, I totally see where you’re coming from, but think about it like this: a one-digit number can represent 10 values, while a two-digit decimal number can represent 100 values. Each extra digit we add doesn’t ten to the cardinality, it it by ten, because the new digit creates ten possible variations of each existing number.

And it’s the same principle here: each binary digit we add multiplies the cardinality by , because that digit can take two values. For example, you could take each of the four 2-bit values from the previous table, and put a “0” bit in front of them, and then you could take them all again and put a “1” bit in front. Thus, the extra bit gives us twice the possibilities: that’s 8 values.

How many numbers can we represent using 8 bits, then—that is, in a Rust ? With one bit, we had 2 possibilities, with two bits, 4, and with three, 8, doubling with each extra bit. So we’ll continue, muttering under our breath, “four bits gives 16, five bits gives 32, six bits gives 64, seven bits gives 128, and eight bits gives 256.”

Okay, so we have 256 possible bit patterns, and if we interpret them as unsigned decimal numbers (“” means “unsigned, 8 bits”), each one can represent a value between 0 and 255 inclusive.

Obvious question, then: what happens if we try to put a number bigger than 255 into a ?

Let’s write a simple Rust program where we do just that. For example:

If we have a variable containing 255, and we try to add 1 to it, then we feel convinced that interesting should happen. Let’s see what:

error: this arithmetic operation will overflow
 --> src/main.rs:3:20
  |
3 |     println!("{}", val + 1);
  |                    ^^^^^^^ attempt to compute `255u8 + 1_u8`, 
  | which would overflow
  |
  = note: `#[deny(arithmetic_overflow)]` on by default

Rust won’t let us even this program, because it’s clear at compile time that the result of the sum won’t fit in 8 bits. That’s helpful, but Rust can’t protect us from every instance of this kind of mistake. It’s not always so clear to the compiler that overflow will happen.

Would you say it’s time to panic?

For example, instead of adding a constant, suppose we use a loop to add increasingly larger numbers to some starting value:

can see that this will soon exceed 255, but I think we’ll be able to sneak that fact past Rust. Let’s find out:

cargo run --example overflow

250 + 1 = 251
250 + 2 = 252
250 + 3 = 253
250 + 4 = 254
250 + 5 = 255

thread 'main' panicked at examples/overflow.rs:4:42:
attempt to add with overflow

Okay. Rust couldn’t catch the problem at build time in this case, but it caught it at run time, which is still better than nothing. At least we didn’t get the wrong answer.

Hang on, though. By default, builds our program using the profile, which behaves slightly differently to the profile. Let’s try it with instead to see what happens:

cargo run --profile release --example overflow

250 + 1 = 251
250 + 2 = 252
250 + 3 = 253
250 + 4 = 254
250 + 5 = 255
250 + 6 = 0

Oh no! It seems like Rust can’t do this simple sum correctly. Before you apply to the Rust Foundation for a refund, though, bear in mind this is documented behaviour, even if it may not be what we intended.

Rust only promises to check for overflow in dev builds. In release builds, these checks are disabled, and the overflowing value : that is, it starts again at the lowest possible value, which in this case is zero.

I care about this because…?

Wrapping an overflowed result is a pragmatic policy, but not always the right one. Imagine yourself on the treatment table of a radiation therapy machine, for example. And let’s say a subtle bug in the dose-calculation software leads to an arithmetic overflow.

Now, what would you prefer to happen next? Choose from one of the following:

  1. The machine stops with an error, requiring the operator to reset it.
  2. The machine gives you an incorrect, fatal dose of radiation.

I can’t imagine any programmer would rather kill the patient than see an error message but, surprisingly, that’s Rust’s default behaviour in this case. (Ironically, my computer crashed right while I was typing that sentence. Food for thought next time you’re trusting your life to someone else’s software.)

Programmers have a term for features like this that make sense in context, but are also easy to misuse or misunderstand, and dangerous when you do: they’re called . In other words, they make it possible to shoot yourself in the foot.

The fact that numbers wrap around in Rust when the operator overflows is just such a footgun. What can we do to avoid a negligent discharge, then? We could try to avoid doing arithmetic at all in our programs, but that’s rather limiting. Is there a better option?

Setting for release builds

As we’ve seen, with the profile Rust will catch overflows for us and stop the program. If you want overflows to be checked with too, or with any other build profile you define, you configure the setting in your :

This is the quickest and simplest way to avoid overflow in production, but it’s not necessarily the way. For one thing, it’s not clear to someone reading your program that overflows will be checked in release mode, if they don’t happen to also glance at your . It’s not the default behaviour, so readers won’t be expecting it.

Also, overflow checks aren’t free. They add significant extra size and run time to the compiled program, and we don’t always need them, so it’s a shame to pay this performance penalty for all arithmetic operations when we don’t have to.

By the way, it’s not only the operator you need to watch out for. The operator can overflow too, since multiplication is just repeated addition.

A similar problem can happen with the operator: if the result of the subtraction is less than the minimum value for the type, it’ll wrap back around to the maximum value (this is called , but it’s the same problem: we ran out of bits).

The , (remainder), (shift left) and (shift right) operators can also overflow on integer types. That’s a whole arsenal of footguns waiting to give us (or our users) a nasty surprise.

Assuming we care about getting our sums right, then, what should we do about this sort of thing? Take a firm grip on your web browser, because I’m about to drop a controversial hot take:

We should avoid using the operator in Rust.

While you’re still reeling from that, I think we should avoid the , , , , and operators too. No matter how wide the data type we use with them, these operators can cause overflow and thus lead to unexpected or non-obvious behaviour.

How on earth are we supposed to do arithmetic in Rust if we shouldn’t use these operators? Well, we have other ways of doing arithmetic. One of the major things Rust does to help us write correct programs is to give us ways to be more about their behaviour.

Arithmetic is a good example of this, because it turns out we can choose exactly the overflow behaviour we want for any particular sum, regardless of the build mode. Let’s go through the available choices one by one.

returns an , which is Rust’s usual way of indicating that there may or may not be a value here.

In this case, if everything’s okay, we’ll get , but if the result of the addition overflowed the type, we’ll get instead:

This is almost certainly what we want in most cases. We’re saying that we don’t this sum to overflow, but it might. If it does, the answer will be invalid , so we don’t want it (we’ll get ). But if everything goes according to plan, we’ll get , and that tells us is valid: there was no overflow.

Here are the checked-arithmetic equivalents for the other operators:

And there are many more methods for other arithmetic operations; have a look at the documentation for , for example, to see the full list.

Sometimes, more rarely, we expect that the sum overflow, and if it does, the answer isn’t necessarily invalid. All the same, we need to know whether overflow has happened, because it may mean that we treat the answer differently.

In this case, we can use . Instead of an , this returns a tuple of two elements: the answer (wrapped or not), and a value that tells us whether overflow occurred:

Again, there are equivalents for the other operators, and the same is true for all the methods we talk about here.

Sometimes we want the number to wrap on overflow, and we don’t need to know whether or not this happened. That’s what the method gives us:

Using makes sense when we the answer to wrap around to its lowest value once it goes past its highest possible value. That’s rare, but there are cases where it’s useful: some kinds of counter or timer use this behaviour, for example.

Making the wrapping explicit helps the reader understand that overflow is expected here, and that it’s the correct behaviour for this particular sum.

Sometimes, rather than wrap the value or return , we want to the result to the maximum value allowed for the type. That’s the behaviour we get from the method:

With our overflow-testing example, this gives:

Obviously this is the wrong answer to this particular sum, but by using we’re that we want either the right answer, the maximum value for a , if the right answer would overflow 8 bits.

For example, suppose our program controls a spacecraft, and its rocket thrust setting is represented as a , meaning that the allowable range is from 0 to 255.

If we’re already at 255—that is, at maximum thrust—and the user presses the “go faster” button again, that’s not an error, but we definitely don’t want the thrust setting to suddenly wrap around to zero! That would give the user a nasty case of whiplash.

The thrust shouldn’t change at all in this case, since it’s already at maximum. To achieve that, we might use to clamp the output to 255 without wrapping.

Sometimes we want to say that a particular sum should overflow in any circumstances, and if that does happen, things have gone so disastrously wrong that the safest course of action is to stop the program (that is, panic). As we’ve seen, that’s what Rust already does implicitly, in dev builds, if we’re using the regular arithmetic operators.

To specify this “panic on overflow” behaviour explicitly, though, we have the method:

In other words, we’re saying that the design of the program should have ensured that overflow never happens, and the fact that it has indicates an unrecoverable bug.

In general, our Rust programs should never panic unless this is the case, but they should always panic when it the case. is the spell we need to ensure that happens.

Choose your own arithmetic adventure

It’s important to be aware of Rust’s default responses to overflow with the traditional arithmetic operators, so let’s tabulate them:

I prefer using explicit arithmetic methods instead: this avoids potential confusion, and makes it clear to readers what will happen if a calculation overflows. To me, this seems very much in the spirit of Rust.

We only want the answer if it’s not wrapped
We treat the answer differently if it’s wrapped
Wrapping is explicitly okay
Answer or , whichever is lowerWe want the answer clamped to

If you want to make sure that you don’t accidentally use one of the forbidden operators—and we all have moments of weakness—there’s a Clippy lint to remind you:

(I’m trying to get this renamed to clippy::operators_of_death, but you’d be surprised how stuffy some people can be about this sort of thing.)

It can sometimes take a bit of extra thought to eliminate unchecked arithmetic in your Rust programs (“What do I want to happen here? Is it okay to wrap? Or should this be an error?”). It’s worthwhile, though, as unhandled overflow can lead to all sorts of unpleasant bugs, including security issues.

In conclusion, if you don’t want to get your bits chopped off—and it’s as painful as it sounds—consider using Rust’s explicit checked arithmetic methods instead of the operators of death.

You can read more valuable medical advice about protecting the health of your programs (and your users) in The Rust Spellbook. Side effects may include better code, a deeper understanding of Rust, and a compulsion to tell people all the interesting stuff you learned. Ask your doctor if the Rust Spellbook is right for you.

items.title: Welcome to the machine: emulating a CPU
items.author: John Arundel
items.content:
Eleven hours and sixteen minutes ago, our scientists lost contact with the Trailblazer 1 probe en route to Proxima Centauri. Since then we’ve been trying without success to re-establish contact with the spacecraft’s onboard computer. If we can’t rectify the problem, we may be faced with a total loss of the vehicle and mission.

That’s why we need your help.

Welcome to the Situation Room. Thank you for coming in at such short notice. Do you have coffee? Okay, then let’s get right to it, because time is a factor.

As you know, the Trailblazer mission is a multi-billion-dollar international scientific collaboration to send a lightsail-powered robotic probe to the Proxima Centauri star system, a journey of about 20 years. The tiny spacecraft, about the size of a smartphone, was launched 15 years ago on a drive beam powered by giant phased laser arrays located in over 40 countries, and reached its coasting velocity of 20% light speed within about 10 minutes, crossing the orbit of Mars half an hour after launch and heading rapidly for the outskirts of the solar system.

For the last 15 years Trailblazer has been sailing serenely through interstellar space, sending back valuable science data and engineering telemetry, as the mission team tested, checked, and rechecked all the onboard instruments in preparation for the probe’s flyby through the Prox Cen system and its many interesting exoplanets.

Then everything went dead.

The binary data modulated onto the optical carrier signal suddenly changed from valid telemetry to a meaningless string of 1s. Since we’re still receiving the signal, we know the spacecraft is intact, powered, and with its communication laser aimed correctly towards Earth. Doppler radar data indicates that its trajectory is unchanged, making it unlikely that the craft was hit by a meteorite or space debris. It’s just no longer able to talk to us.

The problem appears to be localised to a subsystem known as the (Remote Telemetry and Flight Management) computer, responsible for the communications link between the spacecraft and Earth. Engineers are speculating that its memory may have been corrupted by a cosmic ray impact, causing the software to malfunction.

Unfortunately, it seems that while the probe’s computers and flight software were thoroughly documented before launch, that documentation is no longer available, due to… well, let’s just say . We also no longer have the source code or any way to reproduce it. It seems that these files were deleted when one of our cloud drives ran low on space, and everybody thought some department had a copy.

That’s where you come in. We urgently need your help to investigate the RTFM software issue. Specifically, the first thing we need is a program that can execute code written for the spacecraft’s onboard computer.

A program like this is called an : it acts like a model of the computer’s central processing unit (), and will enable us to write and test code before uploading it to the RTFM for real. Time is running out, and there’s no room for mistakes: a botched software update could put the probe out of action for good.

You might also have heard the term , meaning not “nearly a machine”, but something more like “not actually a machine, but behaving like one”. Emulator, virtual machine, same thing.

It sounds complicated, but emulators are actually fairly easy to write, once you understand how the emulated machine (the ) works. The RTFM computer uses a relatively small and simple CPU, compared to the one in your computer (the machine).

This CPU is called the , and to emulate it, you’ll be writing the necessary code to implement the R8’s : the commands it understands. You can use any programming language you like to do this, but we’ve set up starter repos for you for a couple of popular languages:

Sebastián Alvarez has kindly provided a starter repo in TypeScript, too:

These repos will give you the basic structure of the project, plus some tests and stub functions to get you up and running, but after that it’s entirely up to you what to do. So if you want to use a language other than those provided, you could look at one of these repos to get the general idea, and start by implementing it in your language of choice.

The first thing the emulator needs is a properly-initialised CPU, ready to work. So, in the Go repo, for example, there’s an function that returns a CPU in its default initial state, which is specified by a test. In the Rust repo you’ll find an implementation of for the CPU that does the same thing.

The test and the constructor function are already provided in the starter repo, so your first challenge is a straightforward one:

Run the test and make sure it passes.

In Go, for example, run , or in Rust run .

The soul of a new machine

The CPU is the heart of any computer: it does the data processing, executes the software, and controls every other part of the system. Usually made up of many and other electronic components on a , each different model of CPU understands a different : the programming language that tells it what to do.

Machine language consists of commands that mean things like “add this number to this other number”, “read the value at this memory address”, “jump to the program starting at this other address”, and so on.

It’s much than a programming language like Rust: it deals directly with the hardware on the chip. All the same, there are many similarities, and programs in Rust, Go, and other “high-level” languages are usually —automatically translated—into the equivalent , an executable program in machine language.

Putting two and two together

For example, here’s a short program that a CPU such as the R8 might execute:

Can you guess what it does? That’s right, it adds 2 and 2. The (load) instruction puts a number into the CPU’s working area, or scratchpad (known as a ). In this case, it loads the number 2.

Then the instruction adds number to what’s already in the register. In this case, it adds the number 2. The result is that the register will contain the value 4—at least, it will if everything’s working correctly, which it may not be on the Trailblazer spacecraft, but that’s what we’re here to find out.

The R8 doesn’t understand words like or , though: those are (from the Greek for “remember”) designed to be easy for humans to read and write. Actual machine language just consists of numbers.

Every R8 instruction has its own unique identifying number: instruction number 1, instruction number 2, and so on. These are called (for “operation codes”). For example, the opcode for is 16, and the opcode for is 80. (Don’t worry about these particular numbers; they’re basically arbitrary, like phone numbers.)

So the “add 2 and 2” program we just saw actually looks like this in machine language:

You can see why mnemonics were invented! It would be awfully difficult to write programs using only numbers, even though that’s the language that the R8 (like all CPUs) actually speaks. Instead, we use the symbolic names like and , giving us what’s called (I’m not sure why: maybe because writing programs is a bit like putting together IKEA furniture?)

Notice that in order to work out the final result of this program, you had to hold a couple of intermediate results in your head. The CPU does the same thing, by storing them in its working register, which is like your short-term memory. It’s a physical device that lives on the chip itself, and we’ll see how it works in more detail later on, but for now we’re just concerned with the fact that we can store numbers in it.

To that point, we know that R8 are also a sequence of numbers, but unlike the data in the working register, they’re not stored on the chip. So where do these numbers actually live in the computer, and how does the CPU know where to find them?

Another important component of every computer is : also a silicon chip, but a different kind of chip from a CPU. Its job is not to do anything, but just to store numbers: opcodes, operands, science data, images, or anything else we want the computer to handle.

Memory is arranged very simply: it’s just a sequence of —places you can store a number—each with its own , which is also a number. Think of memory addresses as being just like postal addresses. Address 66, for example, is like “Number 66, Memory Lane, Computerville”. What lives at that address? A single piece of —that is, a number.

What that number actually is irrelevant as far as the memory device is concerned. It might be an opcode that’s part of a machine code program, like for a instruction. It might be the operand for such an instruction, like the in . It could be the brightness value of the top left pixel in a camera image of Jupiter. Or it might just be zero, because no meaningful data has been written to that location yet. Whatever the data is in location number , the CPU can retrieve it by asking the memory for the contents of address .

Even though a CPU might seem complicated, and in detail it is, it’s very simple in principle. It just does one thing, over and over, forever:

  1. Fetch the next instruction from memory

It’s called the . And that’s all your emulator needs to do: fetch the next instruction, and execute it. Let’s take the first part first.

Saying ‘the instruction’ implies that the CPU has some way of remembering where we currently ‘are’ in memory. That is to say, we need a CPU register that holds the memory address of the next instruction to execute.

This is what the register is for (PC stands for ‘Program Counter’, which is the traditional name for this register). It keeps count of where the CPU is in the program.

Suppose holds 0, for example. If the CPU were to start running now, the first thing it would do would be to read the contents of memory address 0 (we say that to this address). It will interpret this as an opcode, and do whatever that opcode tells it to do. Afterwards, it will (add 1 to it), and the cycle begins again: the CPU will read the contents of memory address 1, interpret it as an opcode, and… well, you know the rest.

And that’s what your emulator will do, too: perform this fetch-execute cycle continuously. For testing and debugging purposes, though, we’ll start by just fetching and executing instruction at a time. And let’s choose a very easy instruction to implement: the instruction (short for “no operation”). It does nothing!

(Why have such an instruction in the first place, you might ask? Good question, and not every CPU has , but the R8 does. One use for it is just to pass the time, for example if you wanted the machine to wait for a specified delay period without doing anything. Anyway, it’s a good choice for our first emulated instruction.)

We’ll need a way for users to tell the machine to do one iteration of its fetch-execute cycle: fetch the next instruction from memory at the address held by , execute it, and return. So there’s a method on the CPU named that will do this.

Let’s see how we might use it to execute the instruction. First, we’ll create a freshly-initialised CPU. Next, we’ll load the program into its memory. It’s only one instruction long, so we just need to put the opcode for the instruction (which is 1) into some memory location. Since starts at 0, let’s use memory address 0.

Now we call , which will do the following:

  1. Read the contents of memory at the address held by (which is currently 0).
  2. Interpret that value as an opcode, and do what it instructs (the value will be 1, which is the opcode for , so we do nothing).
  3. Increment (so that the CPU will be ready to fetch the next instruction on the next call to ).

So the upshot of all this is that if you call on a machine with pointing to a instruction, the state of the machine should be unchanged after it returns except that the register should hold a value one higher than before.

Uncomment and run the test, which does the following:

  1. Stores the instruction at address 0.
  2. Calls on the machine.
  3. Tests that the machine’s register contains the value 1. If not, the test fails with a message like

This test will not pass yet, because the method currently does nothing. Over to you to fix that!

Write the code in needed to make this test pass. You don’t need much!

You can solve this the “malicious compliance” way if you like, doing literally what the test asks for and no more. Right now the test is only concerned with the value of after calling .

We’ll extend the test later, of course, so if you want to get ahead a little, you could read the contents of memory at the address held by and use something like a statement (in Go) or a expression (in Rust) to decide what to do, as well as updating the value of .

If you’re stuck, or if you want to compare your answer with one suggested version, have a look at my Go solution, or the Rust solution.

You’ll find the TypeScript solutions to each challenge in Sebastián’s ts-r8-solutions repo.

It doesn’t matter if you’ve implemented in a slightly different way to these example solutions, as long as the test passes. After all, the real CPU on the spacecraft implements it using transistors! It’s the behaviour that matters with an emulator, not the implementation.

When the test is passing, you can go on to the next section. Or if you like, pause for tea and biscuits, and some deserved self-congratulation: you’ve written a working CPU emulator! Admittedly, so far it has a rather restricted instruction set, but that can soon be fixed.

The point is that your program accurately models how the real computer works. If it’s executing a program that tells it to do nothing, it obediently does nothing—four million times a second!

Actually, if you were feeling lazy, you could have implemented by writing no more than this (in Go, for example):

You could do more, and if you have, that’s not wrong; but this is all the test actually requires. Since does nothing, and we know the instruction will be , we needn’t even read it from memory. And since the test only checks that is 1 afterwards, we can achieve that by just setting it to that value directly. It might look silly, but it takes the test seriously as the full specification of what it should do.

That’s fine, except we know the real method will need to do more than this. Let’s extend the test, then, so that we can no longer pass it the lazy way.

Extend to store instructions in the first two memory locations, and call , checking for the correct value of after each call. After the first , should be 1, as the test already checks. But after the second , it should be 2.

Adjust to make the test pass.

Updating the test is easy, but if you took the lazy route to implementing , now you’ll have to work a little harder. Even so, you don’t have to actually read the memory or look at the opcode—though you can if you want. The key thing as far as the test is concerned is that should increase by 1 every time is called.

Great. So your test is now executing the following (not particularly interesting, but valid) R8 program:

We could make this program longer, by adding more s, but we’d also need to have the test call again for each one. If we want to execute programs of length, we don’t really want to do it by repeatedly calling in the test.

We’d like a way to tell the CPU to just keep on fetching and executing continuously, as it does in reality. Of course the problem then is, what would make it ?

In reality, CPUs generally don’t stop; they always have work to do, even if it’s just updating the screen, taking care of background jobs like backups, and waiting for you to press a key or click the mouse. But for test purposes, it’ll be very handy for us to have an instruction that tells the CPU to stop work for now, and return control to the emulator. Let’s call it (opcode 0).

Now, what would do? Well, if you call , nothing special. After all, the machine already effectively halts after each call. But we’re saying we want a new method that, unlike , keeps fetching and executing continuously until it sees a instruction, at which point it returns. Let’s call this method (by which we really mean “run ”, of course).

What would a test for look like? You might like to think about this a bit and see if you can come up with something.

Try writing a test for ; don’t actually implement yet, just write an empty method. We want to make sure that the test fails when does nothing.

One way to do it would be to submit a program like this to the CPU:

If we called on this program, we should expect to increase by 2. If it increases by less, or not at all, then isn’t calling enough times. If it increases by too much, or never returns, then isn’t correctly detecting the instruction.

Okay, now let’s try to make the test pass!

We already have code that performs a single fetch-execute cycle, so we don’t need to duplicate it here. can simply call to do that work. The part that needs a little extra thought is this: how does know when to stop running? Or, equivalently, how can report the fact that it executed a instruction?

Again, you could solve this problem a completely different way than I have, and that’s fine. If the emulator correctly executes the test program, it’s correct.

Now we can both and the machine, it’s time to do a little refactoring. We’re going to be referring to opcodes a lot in the emulator, so it’ll be helpful to define some constants for them, with informative names. Here’s a homework problem for you while you’re eagerly awaiting the next instalment.

Define named constants for (0) and (1). Prefixing the names with helps remind readers what of value they are.

Refactor the tests and code to use these constants (for example, in the test, we should set the contents of address 0 to the named constant , instead of a literal .) This makes it easier for readers (including our future selves) to see what the test is doing.

Use the tests to make sure that your refactoring didn’t break anything. Check that you also used the constants in your method. If you like, change the values of the two constants to something different (99 and 100, say) and make sure that everything still passes (it should). Don’t forget to change them back afterwards.

If you get stuck, tune in next time to see the suggested solutions.

Great progress! Your emulator is now looking a lot more realistic: it can be single-stepped, or run until halted. All it needs now to be able to start writing useful programs is a few more opcodes, and we’ll get to those in the next part. If you want to skip ahead and learn a bit about the R8 architecture (and maybe implement more of its instructions), have a look at the RX82 project, which uses it to emulate a fantasy retro 8-bit computer from an alternate 1982.
